options_ranked.title: Base Oil Cost Pass-Through: Non-Anchor Surcharge Plus Queued Anchor Contract Reset
options_ranked.description: Introduce a temporary material-cost adjustment (surcharge or tiered pricing) on Synthetic Blend and Conventional Engine Oil SKUs strictly for non-anchor customers whose contracts permit it — anchor accounts under active price locks are explicitly excluded until their locks expire. Simultaneously initiate formal renegotiation with anchor accounts to reset base prices with cost-indexation clauses effective at lock expiry. Scope targets the degraded Engine Oils line and Value category; segments within threshold are untouched.
options_ranked.rationale: This option pulls the fully confirmed causal chain: base_oil_cost is a confirmed component of COGS, and COGS movement directly moves Gross Margin %. The critic's flag that a surcharge could function as an effective price increase on locked accounts is answered structurally: the surcharge applies only to non-anchor, contractually flexible customers, and anchor recovery is deferred to lock expiry via renegotiation. Adding cost-indexation at renewal prevents the erosion from repeating in the next commodity cycle.

arguments_for: Rests entirely on client-confirmed causal relationships (base_oil_cost -> COGS -> Gross Margin %), making it the most evidentially defensible mechanism on the table.
The surcharge is temporary and reversible, allowing withdrawal if base oil costs normalize without a permanent list-price legacy.
arguments_against: Base oil cost inflation as the dominant driver is inferred from the parallel decline pattern, not yet verified with actual input-cost data — a costing-methodology or allocation artefact would falsify the premise.
Surcharges are commercially visible and may accelerate churn among price-sensitive non-anchor customers in the Value category.
The queued anchor reset delivers nothing in-quarter for locked volume, so in-period recovery depends entirely on non-anchor capture rates.
key_questions: Do non-anchor contracts contain clauses permitting material-cost surcharges, and what share of Engine Oils volume do they cover?
Has base oil input cost actually risen in line with the COGS increase, or is part of the delta an overhead-allocation change?

implementation_triggers: Procurement confirms base oil input cost increase consistent with the COGS delta
Legal confirms surcharge permissibility on non-anchor contracts
prerequisites: Overhead-absorption and allocation-integrity check to rule out a costing-methodology artefact before treating this as a real cost shock
Contractual review segmenting non-anchor volume by surcharge permissibility
Anchor-account renegotiation brief with cost-indexation terms drafted

impact_estimate.basis: Surcharge capture on 50-80% of non-anchor Engine Oils volume plus a queued 1.5-2.5 pp anchor-account reset at lock expiry recovers 3.5-5.8 pp of the 7.14 pp headline decline, sized at the blended enterprise KPI level.

key_assumptions.assumption: The margin decline is driven by real base oil cost inflation flowing into COGS, not an allocation or measurement artefact.
key_assumptions.provenance: Grounded in the client-confirmed base_oil_cost -> COGS and COGS -> Gross Margin % relationships; the inflation magnitude itself is unverified — falsified if procurement data shows flat base oil unit costs over the affected periods.

key_assumptions.assumption: Non-anchor contracts covering a majority of flexible volume legally permit a material-cost surcharge.
key_assumptions.provenance: Legal contract review completing within two weeks; falsified if fewer than 50% of non-anchor contracts permit surcharges.

key_assumptions.assumption: Surcharge introduction does not trigger material volume loss among non-anchor customers.
key_assumptions.provenance: Non-anchor unit volume holding within 5% of baseline for two periods post-surcharge would be consistent with this.

flagged_side_effects: As originally framed, the surcharge could have functioned as an effective mid-quarter price increase on locked anchor accounts, violating the contractual price-lock; the option is now explicitly scoped to non-anchor customers only, with anchor recovery deferred to lock expiry via formal renegotiation.

options_ranked.title: Staged Repricing at Lock Expiry Plus Premium Bundling on Non-Anchor Channels
options_ranked.description: Map anchor accounts whose price-lock clauses expire within 90-180 days and prepare tiered repricing schedules (+3-5% on Synthetic Blend, +2-3% on Conventional) to take effect at renewal. In parallel, run promotional bundling (Synthetic Blend plus premium additive packages) on non-anchor channels to lift realized price/mix without touching locked list prices. Scope is confined to the degraded segments — Synthetic Blend, Conventional, and the Value category; specialty lines and timeframe buckets within threshold are explicitly out of scope.
options_ranked.rationale: The confirmed net_revenue <-> gross_margin_pct relationship means price realization moves the ratio directly. Timing repricing to contractual renewal windows respects the price-lock constraint, and the bundling leg is deliberately positioned as supplemental because the mix-to-margin relationship is an unconfirmed industry prior — the recovery range is anchored on the repricing mechanism, not on mix compounding.

arguments_for: Directly attacks the largest single change point — Synthetic Blend's 7.14 pp margin decline — through the confirmed revenue-to-margin mechanism.
Repricing at renewal windows converts a temporary lock-driven margin trap into a scheduled, contractually clean recovery.
arguments_against: If the decline is purely cost-driven, a +3-5% price move may under-recover unless indexed to base oil cost movements.
The bundling/mix leg rests on an unconfirmed template prior linking premium mix to blended margin, so its contribution could be zero if cost pressure continues to mask mix benefit.
Volume elasticity on repriced accounts could erode the projected 3.2-5.1 pp recovery.
key_questions: What share of Synthetic Blend and Conventional volume sits under locks expiring within 90 days versus 180 days?
What price-elasticity evidence exists from prior repricing cycles on these grades?

implementation_triggers: First anchor-account lock expiry confirmed within 90 days
Price-volume-mix decomposition confirms realized price gap versus cost inflation
prerequisites: Contract register audit identifying lock expiry dates per anchor account
SKU-level price-volume-mix decomposition separating cost inflation from discounting

impact_estimate.basis: Repricing on roughly 60-70% of Synthetic Blend volume post-lock at +3-4% realization, plus bundling-driven mix lift, recovers 3.2-5.1 pp of the observed 7.14 pp Synthetic Blend decline, sized against the blended enterprise KPI.

key_assumptions.assumption: Anchor accounts will accept +3-5% repricing at lock expiry with limited volume loss.
key_assumptions.provenance: Observed renewal-cycle retention: >80% of repriced volume retained two quarters after the first lock-expiry repricing would be consistent with this.

key_assumptions.assumption: Bundling shifts mix toward higher-margin SKUs and that mix shift lifts blended margin.
key_assumptions.provenance: The premium_mix_pct <-> gross_margin_pct link is an unconfirmed template prior; falsified if premium mix rises for two periods while blended margin stays flat or falls.

key_assumptions.assumption: The decline is not primarily discount-driven on non-anchor channels.
key_assumptions.provenance: Price-volume-mix decomposition showing realized price per unit stable while unit COGS rose would confirm; material discount variance would falsify.

flagged_side_effects: The mix-shift leg assumes premium mix lifts blended margin, but that relationship is an unvalidated industry prior — the recovery estimate therefore does not depend on it, and mix contribution should be treated as upside, not base case.

options_ranked.title: Portfolio Reallocation Toward Specialty Formulations, De-Emphasizing Conventional Grade
options_ranked.description: Reallocate sales effort and inventory toward specialty formulations (High Mileage, Compressor Oil) and de-emphasize commodity conventional grades most exposed to base oil pricing. Consistency check: the proposed target segments are themselves under pressure — Compressor Oil fell 5.86 pp (33.86% to 28.00%) and Hydraulic Oil fell 5.76 pp — though Compressor Oil at 28.00% still carries an 8.8 pp absolute margin advantage over Conventional at 19.16%. Step 1 is therefore to stabilize specialty-line margins via the cost pass-through mechanism; Step 2 is to accelerate volume shift only once the absolute margin spread is confirmed durable.
options_ranked.rationale: This questions the frame: if base oil inflation is structural rather than cyclical, defending margin on commodity conventional grades is a losing participation position, and reallocation reduces exposure permanently. The claim that specialty formulations carry lower base-oil intensity is explicitly unvalidated — it rests on the same unconfirmed template prior flagged by the critic — so the option is sequenced to first verify per-unit base-oil intensity and margin durability of the target segments before committing volume. It avoids the price-lock constraint entirely because it changes mix, not locked list prices.

arguments_for: Reduces structural exposure to commodity base oil cycles rather than repeatedly repricing to chase them.
Requires low direct spend — primarily sales-effort and inventory reallocation — with no contractual friction against the anchor price-lock.
arguments_against: The target specialty segments are themselves declining (Compressor Oil -5.86 pp, Hydraulic Oil -5.76 pp), so shifting volume toward them without first stabilizing their margins risks moving the problem, not solving it.
The lower base-oil-intensity premise for specialty formulations is unsupported by any confirmed causal link — the projected uplift is a hypothesis.
Demand-side capacity to absorb 30-40% of conventional volume in specialty categories is unverified and may take multiple quarters to develop.
key_questions: What is the actual base oil content per unit of revenue for High Mileage and Compressor Oil versus Conventional?
Is there demonstrated customer demand to absorb reallocated volume in specialty categories, or does this require new demand creation?

implementation_triggers: Formulation-level bill-of-materials confirms lower base-oil intensity in specialty products
Specialty-line margins stabilize for two consecutive periods after cost pass-through actions
prerequisites: Bill-of-materials analysis quantifying base oil intensity per unit revenue by formulation
Confirmation that Compressor Oil and High Mileage margin declines are cost-driven and recoverable, not demand-driven
Demand assessment for specialty volume absorption by channel

impact_estimate.basis: Reallocating 30-40% of Conventional volume (19.16% margin) toward specialty products at roughly 26-28% margin lifts blended enterprise margin by an estimated 3.2-5.1 pp against the 7.14 pp headline decline; the estimate depends on the specialty margin spread holding, which is a hypothesis, not a confirmed relationship.

key_assumptions.assumption: Specialty formulations carry lower base-oil intensity per unit revenue and therefore reduce blended COGS exposure.
key_assumptions.provenance: Falsified if bill-of-materials analysis shows specialty base-oil content per revenue dollar is comparable to or higher than conventional grades.

key_assumptions.assumption: The absolute margin spread between specialty (26-28%) and conventional (19.16%) grades persists after the current cost shock.
key_assumptions.provenance: Grounded in the change-point data showing Compressor Oil at 28.00% versus Conventional at 19.16% currently; falsified if the spread compresses below 5 pp over the next two periods.

key_assumptions.assumption: Customers will absorb 30-40% of reallocated conventional volume in specialty categories within 12 months.
key_assumptions.provenance: Specialty unit-volume growth of 15%+ within two quarters of reallocation launch would be consistent with this; flat specialty volume would falsify.

flagged_side_effects: The projected margin benefit rests on the unvalidated premise that specialty formulations have lower base-oil intensity — the option is gated on bill-of-materials verification before any volume commitment, and the reallocation is sequenced after specialty-line margins are stabilized, since those target segments are also currently declining.

solutions.recommendation_rationale: The 7.14 pp Synthetic Blend and 6.61 pp Conventional margin declines moved in near-lockstep, which is most consistent with a common COGS driver — and base_oil_cost -> COGS -> Gross Margin % is the only fully client-confirmed causal chain among the three mechanisms proposed. The non-anchor surcharge recovers margin within 30-90 days without touching locked anchor accounts, while the queued contract reset with cost-indexation prevents the erosion from repeating at the next lock cycle. The repricing-at-expiry and portfolio-reallocation options remain valuable sequels, but both lean partly on the unconfirmed premium-mix-to-margin prior, making the cost pass-through the most defensible first move.

problem_reframe.situation: Gross Margin % has dropped 7.14 points to 20.64 year-to-date versus prior year, with the erosion concentrated in Synthetic Blend Engine Oil (-7.14 pp), Conventional Engine Oil (-6.61 pp), and the Value product category (-6.42 pp).
problem_reframe.complication: The compression is synchronized across both premium-blend and conventional grades — pointing to a common input-cost driver flowing through COGS — while the contractual price-lock on Lubricants anchor accounts blocks mid-quarter list-price recovery; meanwhile other portfolio segments and recent timeframe buckets remain within threshold, so this is a concentrated, not universal, problem.
problem_reframe.question: Which combination of cost pass-through, contract-timed repricing, and portfolio mix action recovers the largest share of the 7.14-point Gross Margin % decline without violating the anchor-account price-lock?
key_assumptions: The margin decline is predominantly cost-driven (base oil into COGS) rather than volume/discount-driven — supported by the confirmed base_oil_cost -> COGS -> Gross Margin % chain but not yet decomposed at SKU level.
Anchor-account price locks expire on a knowable schedule within 90-180 days, creating repricing windows.
Segments outside Engine Oils and the Value category are performing within threshold and require no intervention.

unresolved_tensions.tension: Whether the margin decline is a real base oil cost shock or partly a costing/allocation artefact determines if pass-through pricing is justified or would overcharge customers.
unresolved_tensions.requires: Finance controller to complete an overhead-absorption and base oil unit-cost reconciliation for the affected periods before any surcharge is announced (target: end of Week 2).

unresolved_tensions.tension: Portfolio reallocation targets specialty segments (Compressor Oil, Hydraulic Oil) that are themselves declining 5-6 pp, so committing volume there before their margins stabilize could compound the problem.
unresolved_tensions.requires: VP Product to deliver a formulation-level bill-of-materials and margin-durability assessment for High Mileage and Compressor Oil before any sales-effort reallocation begins (target: Week 6).

blind_spots: No customer-level or region-level change points were surfaced — a single large discounting account could be hiding inside the product-level deltas.

The when_signals show large positive deltas in periods 2026-006 through 2026-008 marked within threshold, which sits awkwardly against a decline starting 2026-006; the timing decomposition deserves a second look before attributing the full 7.14 pp to cost inflation.
Competitor pricing response to a surcharge is unmodeled — if competitors absorb the cost shock, non-anchor volume loss could exceed the elasticity assumption.
No procurement/hedging position data was provided; the feasibility of hedging future base oil exposure is assumed, not established.
next_steps: Finance controller to complete base oil unit-cost and overhead-allocation reconciliation for the affected YTD periods, ruling a real cost shock in or out, by end of Week 2.
General counsel to deliver a contract segmentation of Engine Oils volume by surcharge permissibility and anchor lock expiry date by end of Week 2.
VP Sales to draft the non-anchor surcharge schedule and customer communication plan, gated on the Finance reconciliation confirming a real cost shock, by end of Week 4.
Commercial director to prepare anchor-account renegotiation briefs including cost-indexation clauses, ready ahead of the first confirmed lock expiry (by Week 6).
VP Product to complete bill-of-materials base-oil-intensity analysis for High Mileage and Compressor Oil to gate the portfolio reallocation decision by Week 6.

commercial.framework: Price-Volume-Mix Decomposition with Customer Profitability Diagnosis
commercial.hypothesis: Gross margin collapse in Synthetic Blend Engine Oil (−7.14 pp) and Conventional Engine Oil (−6.61 pp) is driven by input cost inflation (base oil and distribution) combined with constrained pricing power due to mid-quarter price-lock contractual clauses on anchor accounts. The 'Value' category segment (−6.42 pp) signals downward mix shift or aggressive discounting on lower-margin SKUs to defend volume.
key_evidence: Synthetic Blend Engine Oil margin fell 7.14 pp (27.78% → 20.64%), the largest product-level delta, despite being positioned as premium tier — inconsistent with mix benefit unless masked by COGS pressure or repricing downward.

Conventional Engine Oil margin fell 6.61 pp (25.77% → 19.16%), tracking within 0.53 pp of Synthetic Blend decline, suggesting a common COGS or pricing driver across both grades rather than isolated product issue.

Value product_category segment declined 6.42 pp (26.24% → 19.82%), indicating either volume shift into lower-margin SKUs or promotional/discount activity to maintain sales velocity in a cost-constrained environment.

operational.framework: Cost-to-Serve Analysis with Input-Cost Hedging Diagnostics
operational.hypothesis: Gross margin compression of 7.14 percentage points in Synthetic Blend Engine Oil is primarily driven by unhedged base oil cost inflation, not revenue price or volume mix. The confirmed DIRECT relationship between base_oil_cost and COGS, combined with the 7.14pp delta concentrated in premium formulations (which carry higher base oil intensity per unit), suggests raw material cost pass-through lag or incomplete cost absorption into selling prices.
